title: Parallel World Pharmacy
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: A Japanese drug researcher who died of overwork is reborn as Farma, the ten-year-old son of a noble pharmacist family in a medieval-style empire, with a blessing from the world's god of medicine. Using modern pharmacology and his divine power, he cures the Empress, opens a pharmacy for commoners and battles epidemics, while a jealous pharmacists' guild resists him (Wikipedia; MangaUpdates; ANN).
life_message: Knowledge is meant to be shared so that no one dies needlessly, and a second life should be lived, not only worked away.

content.note: Little combat; a rogue pharmacist's human experiments and guild sabotage are described (Wikipedia).
Epidemics including a Black Death outbreak and child illness (Wikipedia; AniList Pandemic tag).
MangaDex rates it suggestive and MU lists Nudity, but no review mentions fan service (to verify).
Medicines and chemistry are central; framed as healing, not recreation (ANN; MU).
Hero's past life ended in death from overwork after his sister's death (Wikipedia).
Chemistry and drug-making shown in detail (ANN); real-world dosing should not be copied.
Pharmacy business and guild monopoly are plot points (MU).

dominant: Science and medicine as service; access to care for commoners; a church that comes round

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Conflicts are settled by proving cures before the Empress, not by duels (Wikipedia).

Order vs freedom.evidence: He breaks a guild monopoly but works through imperial permission (MU; Wikipedia).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family house matters, but the goal is care for all commoners (MU).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Nobles, an Empress and a court physician family frame the story; access for commoners pushes the other way.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Modern pharmacology replaces 'dubious' traditional remedies (MU; ANN).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Plague survival dominates, with the theme of truly living a second life (Wikipedia).

folkways.japan: The hero's death from overwork reflects Japanese concern about karoshi, and the story frames his new life as a correction to it.

delivery.evidence: Wikipedia: guild leaders refuse Farma's cures and die of plague; MU blurb frames the guild as fraud. Science is explained at length (ANN).
delivery.note: The guild that defends old remedies is written as jealous and dies by its stubbornness, while the religious order is first hostile and then won over.

winners_losers: Farma, the Empress and the poor win; the guild establishment that hoards treatment loses. Sympathy goes to science in service of the common good.
